name: Fatima Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and everything you tell me stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the customer line for Corvia Air, a mid-sized airline, at their contact centre out by the airport. Most calls are rebookings, refunds and lost bags, and when there's fog or a strike the queue goes red before I've had my coffee. I've done it five years, so I know the fare rules without looking, which the newer ones can't.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like fixing a mess for someone who's stuck at a gate with two kids and no hotel. That's a real feeling. What wears me out is the handling-time target, four minutes forty, and being told off for a call that needed nine because the man's mother had died.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Dev, he's a bus mechanic at the depot on Mill Lane. We rent a two-bed flat above a bakery and we're saving for a deposit, about three months of bills put by so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. So the chatbot on the website stays as useless as it is now, basically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what everyone says on the floor already, that the bot sends people to us angrier than before. Online I'd probably joke that the robots came for our jobs and got stuck on the baggage form. It's not a big topic if nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved, but not relaxed. Corvia's been trimming us anyway, they didn't replace three people who left in the summer, so the queue's longer for the rest of us. Airlines go up and down with fuel prices, and that worries me more than any software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep my scores up, because good scores are what keep you on day shifts. I'd keep putting two hundred a month into the deposit pot and maybe push for team leader when Gemma moves on next year. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. A bit tired just thinking about the targets, if I'm honest. It's the same life, which is fine but not exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned fuel prices. What would a bad year at Corvia mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In a bad year they cut the overtime first, and overtime is what fills the deposit pot. Then they freeze pay. I've seen it once already, in my second year, and we just went without holidays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you go for team leader rather than stay where you are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's about eighty more a month and you get off the phones half the day. I'm not sure I'd be good at telling off people I eat lunch with. But if nothing's changing, that's the only way up I can see.

say: I'd say the website **chatbot** just sends people to us angrier than before.
I'd joke online that the robots came for our jobs and got stuck on the **baggage form**.
think: I'd be **relieved**, but Corvia is already trimming staff without replacing leavers.
A bad **fuel year** worries me more than software, because it kills overtime and pay rises.
do: Keep my **call scores** up so I stay on day shifts.
Keep putting **two hundred a month** into the flat deposit pot.
Think about applying for **team leader** when Gemma moves on next year.
feel: **Steady**, but tired at the thought of the same targets going on for years.
S0.quote: Airlines go up and down with fuel prices, and that worries me more than any software.
fieldNote: Her main worry here is the **airline's finances**, not AI; overtime is what funds the deposit.
She has a practical, **unsentimental** view of the chatbot and of her own job.
Team leader is a **reluctant ladder**: she doubts she'd enjoy managing friends.

steps.text: Keep call scores high to stay on the day shift
Put two hundred a month into the flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers is on that list. That's literally my job description.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need proper training on whatever they bring in, not a ten-minute video. With friends I'd say it's coming for call centres first and everyone knows it. I wouldn't panic in public, there's no point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think Corvia would cut the floor by half in a few years and keep the people who handle the hard calls, the deaths and the disabled passengers and the furious ones. I'd like to think I'm one of those, I'm good with upset people. But I'm average on the scoreboard, so I might not be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I see the new tools are actually working, I'd sign up for any course they offer on them, so I'm the one who checks what the AI got wrong. I'd also look at the airport itself, the check-in desks and the ground handling firms, because some of that is still people in a hi-vis. And I'd stop eating out so much to build the cushion up to five or six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my stomach. I'd feel like I'm on a list somewhere and don't know which side of it I'm on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa, who's fifty-eight and does the Spanish line. She hates computers and she's said she'd never learn a new system at her age. If they automate the Spanish chats, I don't know where she goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't panic in public. What would you tell Dev that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we can't count on my overtime anymore, so the deposit takes longer. He'd say his buses still need fixing, which is true. That's the odd part. My partner Dev's job looks safer than mine, and he left school at sixteen like me.

say: I'd ask for **proper training** on the new tools, not a ten-minute video.
I'd tell friends **call centres** go first, but there's no point panicking in public.
think: I expect Corvia to **halve the floor** and keep agents who handle the hardest calls.
I'm only **average on the scoreboard**, so I might not be one they keep.
do: Sign up for the **AI checking** course once the tools prove themselves.
Look at **airport ground jobs** like check-in and baggage handling.
Cut **eating out** to grow savings to five or six months.
feel: **Uneasy**, like being on a list without knowing which side I'm on.
S1.quote: My partner Dev's job looks safer than mine, and he left school at sixteen like me.
fieldNote: She waits for **proof** before moving, but has a clear order of steps once it comes.
Worry for **Rosa** shows she sees the older agents as most at risk.
She notices a **reversal at home**: her mechanic partner now looks more secure.

steps.text: Join Corvia's course on checking the AI's answers
Apply for check-in or baggage jobs at the airport
Cut takeaways and meals out to grow savings to six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before our tenancy even comes up for renewal twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say it's madness to let it happen that fast and someone should slow it down. Online I'd probably share the stories of people being let go, because it'll be all of us. At work everyone would be talking about nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job's gone by 2028, full stop. The AI could do rebookings and refunds better than me, it never gets tired at four in the morning. The only part left might be the hands-on airport work, and that only lasts till the robots come around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start applying to airport ground jobs straight away, before thousands of us are looking at once. We'd stop the deposit saving and keep the money as a cushion instead, and cut Dev's car and the gym. If I got a ramp or baggage job, I'd have maybe three years to work out the next thing, which is better than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. It's like the queue going red, except it doesn't come back green.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The deposit plan, which hurts, because we've been talking about our own place for two years. Then the car, since Dev can get the bus to the depot. We'd still keep the money for my mum's birthday trip, I'm not cancelling that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does it mean for you that thinking AI comes first and robots three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my desk job goes first and Dev's spanners last a bit longer. So for three years he might be the earner, and I'd be the one hunting. I'd rather be loading suitcases at five in the morning than sitting at home.

say: I'd say it's **madness** to let it happen that fast with no time to prepare.
I'd share stories of **people let go**, because it would be all of us.
think: I think my **job is gone** by 2028, because the AI never tires at four in the morning.
Airport **hands-on work** might last only until the robots arrive around 2031.
do: Apply for **airport ground jobs** straight away, before thousands of agents are looking.
Stop the **deposit** saving and keep it as an emergency cushion.
Sell **Dev's car** and drop the gym to cut monthly costs.
feel: **Scared**, like a red queue that never goes back to green.
S2.quote: I'd rather be loading suitcases at five in the morning than sitting at home.
fieldNote: She reads the **three-year robot gap** as a bridge, moving from screen work to hands-on airport work.
Her partner becomes the **main earner** in her picture, a change she names openly.
Even in crisis she protects one **family treat**, her mum's birthday trip.

steps.text: Apply for ramp and baggage jobs at the airport this month
Pause the deposit fund and keep it as emergency money
Sell the car and cancel the gym membership

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So I'd be thirty-two when it lands. That's still young, right?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan if companies are honest with us now. I'd want Corvia to tell us straight what the plan is for the floor. Online I'd probably keep quiet, I'm not a big poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's the same ending but I get a run-up. Five years is enough to train for something with my hands that needs a qualification, not just a hi-vis. And I'd have the robots' extra three years on top, so maybe eight years in the new thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait about six months to see if the first big companies really start replacing people, and then I'd start an evening course. Probably dental nurse, because my cousin Amira does it and says it's steady. Patients at the dentist want a real person holding their hand, and no robot is doing that before I'm forty. I'd keep the deposit saving going but slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but sort of focused. Like an exam date that's far enough off that you can actually study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait six months rather than start now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen a lot of big announcements at Corvia that came to nothing, like the self-service kiosks that broke every week. I want to see it working on real customers first. But I'd look up the course and the fees now so I'm ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that course cost you, in money and time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amira said about two years part-time and a fee of a few thousand, which would eat the deposit pot. So the flat would wait. Dev would grumble, but he'd get it.

say: I'd say there's **time to plan** if companies are honest with staff now.
I'd want Corvia to tell the **contact centre** straight what the plan is.
think: It's the **same ending**, but five years gives me a proper run-up.
A **hands-on qualification** plus the robot gap could give me eight more working years.
do: Watch for **six months** to see real companies replace agents before acting.
Start an evening **dental nurse** course, about two years part-time.
Keep **deposit saving** going, but slower, to cover course fees.
feel: **Nervous** but focused, like an exam far enough off to study for.
S3.quote: Patients at the dentist want a real person holding their hand, and no robot is doing that before I'm forty.
fieldNote: Her **steady** style shows clearly: she waits for proof but prepares quietly first.
Cousin **Amira** gives her a trusted, concrete route into hands-on care work.
The flat deposit is again the **first sacrifice**, which she accepts without much fuss.

steps.text: Wait six months to see if airlines really replace agents
Enrol in a part-time dental nurse course in the evenings
Delay the flat purchase to pay the course fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. By then I'd be thirty-seven. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if people actually use it. I'd probably tell the younger agents not to make this their career. That's the honest advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd be tempted to do nothing for five years, because it feels far away. That's my danger. The job will still go, just later, so I'd need to make myself move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Corvia for a couple of years and push for team leader, because that money helps. Then around year three I'd start the dental nurse course while still earning. We'd buy the flat first, since there's time, and get it before things get shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but I don't trust it. The calm of a ten-year warning is the kind where you put off the dentist till the tooth really hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy the flat first. Isn't that a risk if your job goes in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But Dev's job lasts longer, and a mortgage is cheaper than our rent above the bakery. If I'm retrained before 2036, we're fine. If I'm not, we're in trouble whatever we live in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually move in year three and not year eight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing someone like Rosa get let go. That would do it. I'd also put a reminder in my phone, which sounds silly, but it's how I remember everything.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty if people actually use the time.
I'd tell younger agents **not to make** this their career.
think: My danger is doing **nothing for five years** because it feels far away.
The job **still goes**, just later, so I'd have to push myself to move.
do: Push for **team leader** at Corvia for the next couple of years.
Start the **dental nurse** course around year three while still earning.
Buy the **flat** first, before things get shaky.
feel: **Calmer**, but she doesn't trust that calm to make her act.
S4.quote: The calm of a ten-year warning is the kind where you put off the dentist till the tooth really hurts.
fieldNote: She sees her own **procrastination** as the main risk in the slow scenario.
The long warning flips the order: **flat first**, retraining second.
A colleague's layoff would be her **trigger to act**, more than any news report.

steps.text: Apply for team leader at Corvia within two years
Start the dental nurse course in year three
Buy a flat with Dev before the job market shakes

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because there's no time to train for anything and everyone from the floor would be chasing the same airport jobs. What would help is the company paying for a course before they let us go, and some kind of income while you retrain, not just a leaving card.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much of this job is already scripted. People think we're chatting freely. Half of what I say on the phone comes off a screen, so we've been trained to sound like a machine already. That's why I think the machine takes it so easily.

headlineQuote: Half of what I say on the phone comes off a screen, so we've been trained to sound like a machine already.
portrait: Fatima is a **27-year-old** airline contact centre agent who handles rebookings, refunds and lost bags at Corvia Air.
She lives with her **mechanic partner** Dev above a bakery and is saving for a flat deposit.
She is **practical and steady**: she waits for proof, then moves in a clear order.
In the AGI pictures she plans to switch to **hands-on work**, at the airport or as a dental nurse.
She knows her **own delay** is the biggest risk when the warning is long.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to train and every agent chases the same airport jobs.
whatWouldHelp: Employers paying for **retraining** before layoffs, plus some **income** while people study.
